claim: N6-methyladenosine (m6A) is an abundant mRNA modification and affects many biological processes.
source: N6-methyladenosine (m6A) is an abundant mRNA modification and affects many biological processes.
evidence: This is a general statement about m6A that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Rotavirus infection induced global m6A modifications on mRNA transcripts by down-regulating the m6a eraser ALKBH5.
source: We found that rotavirus infection induced global m6A modifications on mRNA transcripts by down-regulating the m6a eraser ALKBH5.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in the manuscript including dot blot, mass spectrometry, and Western blot analyses.

claim: Mice lacking the m6A writer enzymes METTL3 in IECs (Mettl3ΔIEC) were resistant to RV infection.
source: Mice lacking the m6A writer enzymes METTL3 in IECs (Mettl3ΔIEC) were resistant to RV infection and showed increased expression of interferons (IFNs) and IFN-stimulated genes (ISGs).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo mouse infection studies showing reduced viral loads.

claim: Mettl3ΔIEC mice showed increased expression of interferons (IFNs) and IFN-stimulated genes (ISGs).
source: Mice lacking the m6A writer enzymes METTL3 in IECs (Mettl3ΔIEC) were resistant to RV infection and showed increased expression of interferons (IFNs) and IFN-stimulated genes (ISGs).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data and RNA-sequencing data presented in the manuscript.

claim: IRF7 is one of the primary m6A targets during virus infection.
source: Using RNA-sequencing and m6A RNA immuno-precipitation (RIP)-sequencing, we identified IRF7, a master regulator of IFN responses, as one of the primary m6A targets during virus infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by m6A-RIP-sequencing and RNA-sequencing data presented in the manuscript.

claim: IRF7 is a master regulator of IFN responses.
source: Using RNA-sequencing and m6A RNA immuno-precipitation (RIP)-sequencing, we identified IRF7, a master regulator of IFN responses, as one of the primary m6A targets during virus infection.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature in the field.

claim: In the absence of METTL3, IECs showed increased Irf7 mRNA stability.
source: In the absence of METTL3, IECs showed increased Irf7 mRNA stability and enhanced type I and III IFN expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA degradation assays using actinomycin D treatment.

claim: In the absence of METTL3, IECs showed enhanced type I and III IFN expression.
source: In the absence of METTL3, IECs showed increased Irf7 mRNA stability and enhanced type I and III IFN expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data measuring IFN expression levels.

claim: Deficiency in IRF7 attenuated the elevated expression of IFNs and ISGs in Mettl3ΔIEC mice.
source: Deficiency in IRF7 attenuated the elevated expression of IFNs and ISGs and restored susceptibility to RV infection in Mettl3ΔIEC mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data from double knockout mice (Irf7−/−Mettl3ΔIEC).

claim: Deficiency in IRF7 restored susceptibility to RV infection in Mettl3ΔIEC mice.
source: Deficiency in IRF7 attenuated the elevated expression of IFNs and ISGs and restored susceptibility to RV infection in Mettl3ΔIEC mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by viral load measurements in double knockout mice.

claim: The global m6A modification on mRNA transcripts declined with age in mice, with a significant drop from 2 weeks to 3 weeks post birth.
source: Moreover, the global m6A modification on mRNA transcripts declined with age in mice, with a significant drop from 2 weeks to 3 weeks post birth, which likely has broad implications for the development of intestinal immune system against enteric viruses early in life.
evidence: This claim is supported by m6A dot blot and mass spectrometry data from mice of different ages.

claim: The decline in m6A modifications with age likely has broad implications for the development of intestinal immune system against enteric viruses early in life.
source: Moreover, the global m6A modification on mRNA transcripts declined with age in mice, with a significant drop from 2 weeks to 3 weeks post birth, which likely has broad implications for the development of intestinal immune system against enteric viruses early in life.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed age-dependent decline in m6A modifications.

claim: m6A is the most abundant internal mRNA modification.
source: N6-methyladenosine (m6A) is the most abundant internal mRNA modification and modulates diverse cellular functions through m6A-related writers, erasers, and readers (Roundtree et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2021; Chelmicki et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: m6A modulates diverse cellular functions through m6A-related writers, erasers, and readers.
source: N6-methyladenosine (m6A) is the most abundant internal mRNA modification and modulates diverse cellular functions through m6A-related writers, erasers, and readers (Roundtree et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2021; Chelmicki et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The m6A modification directly recruits m6A-specific proteins of the YT521-B homology (YTH) domain family.
source: The m6A modification directly recruits m6A-specific proteins of the YT521-B homology (YTH) domain family (Roundtree et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: YTH domain family proteins mediate the m6A-dependent regulation of pre-mRNA processing, microRNA processing, translation initiation, and mRNA decay.
source: These proteins mediate the m6A-dependent regulation of pre-mRNA processing, microRNA processing, translation initiation, and mRNA decay (Roundtree et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: m6A modifications have been identified in the genomes of RNA viruses and the transcripts of DNA viruses with either a pro-viral or anti-viral role.
source: In recent works, m6A modifications has been identified in the genomes of RNA viruses and the transcripts of DNA viruses with either a pro-viral or anti-viral role (Tsai et al., 2018; Li et al., 2017; Hesser et al., 2018; Imam et al., 2018; Ye et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: m6A RNA modification-mediated down-regulation of the α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase (KGDH)-itaconate pathway inhibits viral replication independent of the innate immune response.
source: Furthermore, m6A RNA modification-mediated down-regulation of the α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase (KGDH)-itaconate pathway inhibits viral replication independent of the innate immune response (Liu, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: m6A modification preserves the self-recognition of endogenous transcripts.
source: According to Gao et al., 2020, m6A modification preserves the self-recognition of endogenous transcripts.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Deletion of the m6A writer Mettl3 decreases the m6A modifications in endogenous retrovirus (ERV) transcripts.
source: Deletion of the m6A writer Mettl3 decreases the m6A modifications in endogenous retrovirus (ERV) transcripts.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Gao et al., 2020.

claim: The accumulation of ERVs activates pattern recognition receptors (e.g. RIG-I) pathways, resulting in a detrimental interferon response in livers of fetal mice.
source: The accumulation of ERVs activates pattern recognition receptors (e.g. RIG-I) pathways, resulting in a detrimental interferon response in livers of fetal mice (Gao et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The m6A modification of the enterovirus 71 (EV71) RNA genome is important for viral propagation.
source: The m6A modification of the enterovirus 71 (EV71) RNA genome is important for viral propagation, and EV71 infection increases the expression of m6A writers in vitro (Hao et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: EV71 infection increases the expression of m6A writers in vitro.
source: The m6A modification of the enterovirus 71 (EV71) RNA genome is important for viral propagation, and EV71 infection increases the expression of m6A writers in vitro (Hao et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: m6A methyltransferase METTL3 knockdown reduces EV71 replication.
source: m6A methyltransferase METTL3 knockdown reduces whereas m6A demethylase FTO knockdown increases EV71 replication (Hao et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: m6A demethylase FTO knockdown increases EV71 replication.
source: m6A methyltransferase METTL3 knockdown reduces whereas m6A demethylase FTO knockdown increases EV71 replication (Hao et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Human cytomegalovirus can upregulate the expression of m6A-related proteins.
source: In addition, human cytomegalovirus can upregulate the expression of m6A-related proteins (Rubio et al., 2018; Winkler et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The regulation of m6A modifications and the specific role of m6A in the antiviral response in vivo, especially in the gastrointestinal tract, remains unclear.
source: Despite the knowledges about m6A regulation and function during viral infection revealed by these in vitro studies, the regulation of m6A modifications and the specific role of m6A in the antiviral response in vivo, especially in the gastrointestinal tract, remains unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in knowledge that the current study aims to address.

claim: Rotavirus (RV) is a member of the family Reoviridae.
source: Rotavirus (RV), a member of the family Reoviridae, is a nonenveloped icosahedral-structured virus with 11 segments of double-stranded RNA.
evidence: This is established knowledge about rotavirus classification.

claim: Rotavirus is a nonenveloped icosahedral-structured virus with 11 segments of double-stranded RNA.
source: Rotavirus (RV), a member of the family Reoviridae, is a nonenveloped icosahedral-structured virus with 11 segments of double-stranded RNA.
evidence: This is established knowledge about rotavirus structure.

claim: Children under the age of five are at high risk of rotavirus infection, which causes severe diarrhea, dehydration, and death.
source: Children under the age of five are at high risk of rotavirus infection, which causes severe diarrhea, dehydration, and death (Crawford et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Rotaviruses encode multiple viral proteins to inhibit innate immune responses by degrading interferon regulatory factors (IRFs) and mitochondrial antiviral-signaling protein (MAVS).
source: Rotaviruses encode multiple viral proteins to inhibit innate immune responses by degrading interferon regulatory factors (IRFs) and mitochondrial antiviral-signaling protein (MAVS), thus facilitating efficient virus infection and replication (Ding et al., 2018; Barro and Patton, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The timely induction of an IFN response is key to the host successful control of invading viruses, including RV.
source: The timely induction of an IFN response is key to the host successful control of invading viruses, including RV (Honda et al., 2005; Lin et al., 2016; Pott et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: RV infections primarily take place in children under the age of five in humans and in neonatal mice younger than 2 weeks old.
source: RV infections primarily take place in children under the age of five in humans and in neonatal mice younger than 2 weeks old (Crawford et al., 2017; Du et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Total RNA m6A modifications in the mouse ileal tissues significantly declined from 2 weeks to 3 weeks post birth.
source: Intriguingly, total RNA m6A modifications in the mouse ileal tissues, revealed by a m6A dot blot and mass spectrum (MS) analysis, significantly declined from 2 weeks to 3 weeks post birth (Figure 1a, b and c), which caused by increased Alkbh5 expression (Figure 1d, Figure 1—figure supplement 1a and Figure 1—figure supplement 1b) and development of microbiota might be involved (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by m6A dot blot and mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The decline in m6A modifications from 2 to 3 weeks post birth was caused by increased Alkbh5 expression.
source: Intriguingly, total RNA m6A modifications in the mouse ileal tissues, revealed by a m6A dot blot and mass spectrum (MS) analysis, significantly declined from 2 weeks to 3 weeks post birth (Figure 1a, b and c), which caused by increased Alkbh5 expression (Figure 1d, Figure 1—figure supplement 1a and Figure 1—figure supplement 1b) and development of microbiota might be involved (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR and Western blot data showing increased Alkbh5 expression.

claim: Development of microbiota might be involved in the decline of m6A modifications with age.
source: Intriguingly, total RNA m6A modifications in the mouse ileal tissues, revealed by a m6A dot blot and mass spectrum (MS) analysis, significantly declined from 2 weeks to 3 weeks post birth (Figure 1a, b and c), which caused by increased Alkbh5 expression (Figure 1d, Figure 1—figure supplement 1a and Figure 1—figure supplement 1b) and development of microbiota might be involved (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on data from germ-free mice.

claim: Overexpression of Alkbh5 in mouse IEC cell line caused decreased m6A level.
source: Indeed, overexpression of Alkbh5 in mouse IEC cell line caused decreased m6A level (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c), supporting the role of Alkbh5 in regulating global m6A levels in intestine.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c.

claim: The global m6A RNA modification levels increased in the ileum tissue of suckling mice post RV murine strain EW infection.
source: Besides, the global m6A RNA modification levels increased in the ileum tissue of suckling mice post RV murine strain EW infection (Figure 1e and f and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by m6A dot blot and mass spectrometry data shown in the figures.

claim: The m6A modification can barely be detected in IECs deficient with m6A writer METTL3 (Mettl3fl/flVil1Cre, Mettl3ΔIEC).
source: As a control, the m6A modification can barely detected in IECs deficiency with m6A writer METTL3 (Mettl3fl/flVil1Cre, Mettl3ΔIEC) (Figure 1e and f).
evidence: This claim is supported by m6A dot blot data shown in Figure 1e and f.

claim: The viral RNA load in Mettl3ΔIEC mice ileum tissue was significantly lower than that in the WT mice.
source: The viral RNA load in Mettl3ΔIEC mice ileum tissue was significantly lower than that in the WT mice (Figure 1g and Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data measuring viral loads shown in the figures.

claim: Fecal virus shedding was significantly lower in Mettl3ΔIEC mice.
source: Fecal virus shedding was also significantly lower in Mettl3ΔIEC mice (Figure 1h).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data measuring fecal viral shedding shown in Figure 1h.

claim: Genetic knockdown of METTL3 in HT-29 cells by CRISPR-mediated gene silencing led to reduced RV replication.
source: Genetic knockdown of METTL3 in HT-29 cells, a human colonic epithelial cell line, by CRISPR-mediated gene silencing, also led to reduced RV replication (Figure 1i), further highlighting the resistance phenotype to RV infection by METTL3 deficiency.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data from in vitro cell culture experiments shown in Figure 1i.

claim: Most of the differentially expressed genes in METTL3-deficient IECs vs WT IECs were enriched in the pathways of 'defense response to virus', 'response to interferon-beta', and 'positive regulation of innate immune response'.
source: Most of the differentially expressed genes in METTL3-deficient IECs vs WT IECs were enriched in the pathways of 'defense response to virus', 'response to interferon-beta', and 'positive regulation of innate immune response' by gene ontology analysis (Figure 2a).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: A panel of interferon stimulate genes (ISGs) are upregulated in METTL3-deficient IECs compared to WT IECs.
source: Heatmap also showed that a panel of interferon stimulate genes (ISGs) are upregulated in METTL3-deficient IECs compared to WT IECs (Figure 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in a heatmap in Figure 2b.

claim: m6A modified Irf7.
source: We found that m6A modified one of the master regulators of IFNs, Irf7 (Figure 2c), which played a key role in the network of these differential expressed genes in METTL3-deficient IECs compared to WT IECs, analyzed by STRING (Figure 2d).
evidence: This claim is supported by m6A-RIP-seq data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Irf7 played a key role in the network of differentially expressed genes in METTL3-deficient IECs compared to WT IECs.
source: We found that m6A modified one of the master regulators of IFNs, Irf7 (Figure 2c), which played a key role in the network of these differential expressed genes in METTL3-deficient IECs compared to WT IECs, analyzed by STRING (Figure 2d).
evidence: This claim is supported by STRING network analysis shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Irf7 was the only IRF that was highly expressed in METTL3-deficient IECs.
source: Of note, Irf7 was the only IRFs that highly expressed in METTL3-deficient IECs, and Irf7 was the prominently highest expressed Irf in IECs (Figure 2e), indicating Irf7 might be one of the key genes that are modulated by m6A modifications.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Irf7 was the prominently highest expressed Irf in IECs.
source: Of note, Irf7 was the only IRFs that highly expressed in METTL3-deficient IECs, and Irf7 was the prominently highest expressed Irf in IECs (Figure 2e), indicating Irf7 might be one of the key genes that are modulated by m6A modifications.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: The m6A peak is enriched near the stop codon and 3'-UTR region.
source: Metagene plots showed the m6A peak is enriched near the stop codon and 3'-UTR region, which is consistent with previously studies (Xuan et al., 2018; Dominissini et al., 2012; Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by m6A-RIP-seq data and citations to previous literature.

claim: There was an increase of Irf7 mRNA in ileum tissue of Mettl3ΔIEC mice compared to that in WT littermate control mice.
source: We found an increase of Irf7 mRNA in ileum tissue of Mettl3ΔIEC mice compared to that in WT littermate control mice (Figure 2f).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: The expression of IRF7 mRNA was higher in METTL3 knockdown HT-29 and METTL3 knockout rhesus monkey MA104 cells.
source: Consistently, the expression of IRF7 mRNA was also higher in METTL3 knockdown HT-29 and METTL3 knockout rhesus monkey MA104 cells, suggesting that the regulation of IRF7/Irf7 expression by m6A is likely conserved across species (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data from cell culture experiments shown in the supplementary figures.

claim: The regulation of IRF7/Irf7 expression by m6A is likely conserved across species.
source: Consistently, the expression of IRF7 mRNA was also higher in METTL3 knockdown HT-29 and METTL3 knockout rhesus monkey MA104 cells, suggesting that the regulation of IRF7/Irf7 expression by m6A is likely conserved across species (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an inference based on data from multiple species (mouse, human, rhesus monkey).

claim: Genetic knockdown of METTL3 in human or mice IEC cell lines led to increased IRF7/Irf7 expression and IFN/Ifn responses.
source: Furthermore, genetic knockdown of METTL3 in human or mice IEC cell lines also led to increased IRF7/Irf7 expression and IFN/Ifn responses (Figure 2—figure supplement 1f, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot and qPCR data shown in the supplementary figures.

claim: The IRF7 mRNA degraded significantly slower in METTL3-knockdown HT-29 cells than the control cell line.
source: The IRF7 mRNA degraded significantly slower in METTL3-knockdown HT-29 cells than the control cell line (Figure 2g, Figure 2—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA degradation assay data using actinomycin D shown in Figure 2g.

claim: The ectopically expressed constructs harboring m6A mutant Irf7-3'UTR (Irf7-MUT) showed significantly increased luciferase activity compared with wild-type Irf7-3'UTR (Irf7-WT) constructs.
source: In comparison with wild-type Irf7-3'UTR (Irf7-WT) constructs, the ectopically expressed constructs harboring m6A mutant Irf7-3'UTR (Irf7-MUT) showed significantly increased luciferase activity (Figure 2h, Figure 2—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 2h.

claim: Mutation of m6A modification sites can directly increase the expression of Irf7 and enhance the antiviral function of Irf7 in MEF cells.
source: Further, mutation of m6A modification sites can directly increase the expression of Irf7 and enhance the antiviral function of Irf7 in MEF cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 4a and Figure 2—figure supplement 4b).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR and Western blot data from MEF cells shown in the supplementary figures.

claim: The transcriptional targets of Irf7 were all upregulated in Mettl3ΔIEC mice.
source: We found the transcriptional targets of Irf7, were all upregulated in Mettl3ΔIEC mice (Figure 2i).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data measuring IFNs and ISGs shown in Figure 2i.

claim: The mRNAs of Irf7 and its transcriptional targets ISGs increased in the ileum of the mice from 1 to 4 weeks, with a dramatic upregulation from 2 to 3 weeks.
source: Furthermore, we found that the mRNAs of Irf7 and its transcriptional targets ISGs increased in the ileum of the mice from 1 to 4 weeks, with a dramatic upregulation from 2 to 3 weeks (Figure 2—figure supplement 5), which was concomitant with the decrease of global m6A modifications (Figure 1a and b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: The increase in Irf7 and ISG mRNAs from 2 to 3 weeks was concomitant with the decrease of global m6A modifications.
source: Furthermore, we found that the mRNAs of Irf7 and its transcriptional targets ISGs increased in the ileum of the mice from 1 to 4 weeks, with a dramatic upregulation from 2 to 3 weeks (Figure 2—figure supplement 5), which was concomitant with the decrease of global m6A modifications (Figure 1a and b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal correlation between two sets of data.

claim: The expression of IFNs and ISGs in ileum from Irf7−/−Mettl3ΔIEC mice were significantly lower than those from Mettl3ΔIEC mice at 2dpi.
source: Following RV oral gavage, the expression of IFNs and ISGs in ileum from Irf7−/−Mettl3ΔIEC mice were significantly lower than those from Mettl3ΔIEC mice at 2dpi (Figure 3a–c), and unlike the increased expression of IFNs and ISGs in Mettl3ΔIEC mice vs littermate WT controls, by deficiency of IRF7, the expression of IFNs and ISGs in ileum from Irf7−/−Mettl3ΔIEC mice were not significantly different from those from Irf7−/− mice (Figure 3a–c), suggesting that Irf7 mediates the increased expression of IFNs and ISGs in Mettl3ΔIEC mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data from double knockout mice shown in Figure 3a-c.

claim: The expression of IFNs and ISGs in ileum from Irf7−/−Mettl3ΔIEC mice were not significantly different from those from Irf7−/− mice.
source: Following RV oral gavage, the expression of IFNs and ISGs in ileum from Irf7−/−Mettl3ΔIEC mice were significantly lower than those from Mettl3ΔIEC mice at 2dpi (Figure 3a–c), and unlike the increased expression of IFNs and ISGs in Mettl3ΔIEC mice vs littermate WT controls, by deficiency of IRF7, the expression of IFNs and ISGs in ileum from Irf7−/−Mettl3ΔIEC mice were not significantly different from those from Irf7−/− mice (Figure 3a–c), suggesting that Irf7 mediates the increased expression of IFNs and ISGs in Mettl3ΔIEC mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data from double knockout mice shown in Figure 3a-c.

claim: Irf7 mediates the increased expression of IFNs and ISGs in Mettl3ΔIEC mice.
source: Following RV oral gavage, the expression of IFNs and ISGs in ileum from Irf7−/−Mettl3ΔIEC mice were significantly lower than those from Mettl3ΔIEC mice at 2dpi (Figure 3a–c), and unlike the increased expression of IFNs and ISGs in Mettl3ΔIEC mice vs littermate WT controls, by deficiency of IRF7, the expression of IFNs and ISGs in ileum from Irf7−/−Mettl3ΔIEC mice were not significantly different from those from Irf7−/− mice (Figure 3a–c), suggesting that Irf7 mediates the increased expression of IFNs and ISGs in Mettl3ΔIEC mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic rescue experiment data.

claim: The Irf7−/−Mettl3ΔIEC mice showed significantly higher viral loads in ileum tissue than Mettl3ΔIEC mice.
source: Moreover, the Irf7−/−Mettl3ΔIEC mice showed significantly higher viral loads in ileum tissue and higher fecal shedding of RV Mettl3ΔIEC (Figure 3d–f).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data measuring viral loads shown in Figure 3d-f.

claim: The Irf7−/−Mettl3ΔIEC mice showed higher fecal shedding of RV than Mettl3ΔIEC mice.
source: Moreover, the Irf7−/−Mettl3ΔIEC mice showed significantly higher viral loads in ileum tissue and higher fecal shedding of RV Mettl3ΔIEC (Figure 3d–f).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data measuring fecal viral shedding shown in Figure 3d-f.

claim: The fecal viral shedding in Irf7−/−Mettl3ΔIEC mice were not significantly different from those in Irf7−/− mice.
source: Similarly, unlike the much lower fecal viral shedding in Mettl3ΔIEC mice vs littermate WT controls, by deficiency of IRF7, the fecal viral shedding in Irf7−/−Mettl3ΔIEC mice were not significantly different from those in Irf7−/− mice (Figure 3d), suggesting that Irf7 mediates the resistant phenotype of rotavirus infection measured by fecal viral shedding in Mettl3ΔIEC mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Irf7 mediates the resistant phenotype of rotavirus infection measured by fecal viral shedding in Mettl3ΔIEC mice.
source: Similarly, unlike the much lower fecal viral shedding in Mettl3ΔIEC mice vs littermate WT controls, by deficiency of IRF7, the fecal viral shedding in Irf7−/−Mettl3ΔIEC mice were not significantly different from those in Irf7−/− mice (Figure 3d), suggesting that Irf7 mediates the resistant phenotype of rotavirus infection measured by fecal viral shedding in Mettl3ΔIEC mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic rescue experiment data.

claim: Besides the contribution of Irf7 to the resistant phenotype of rotavirus infection in IECs from Mettl3ΔIEC mice, other pathways (e.g. m6A modifications in RV RNA) may also play roles.
source: Notably, the viral proteins expression difference in ileum from Irf7−/−Mettl3ΔIEC mice vs that from Irf7−/− mice (9.7-fold lower for NSP2 and 9.3-fold lower for VP7), was much lower than the viral proteins expression difference in ileum from Mettl3ΔIEC mice vs that from littermate mice (267.1-fold lower for NSP2 and 283.4-fold lower for VP7) (Figure 3e), suggesting that besides the contribution of Irf7 to the resistant phenotype of rotavirus infection in IECs from Mettl3ΔIEC mice, other pathways (e.g. m6A modifications in RV RNA) may also play roles.
evidence: This is an inference based on the incomplete rescue of the phenotype by IRF7 deficiency.

claim: IRF7 is an important mediator of the increased IFNs and ISGs expression in Mettl3ΔIEC mice.
source: Therefore, IRF7 is an important mediator of the increased IFNs and ISGs expression in Mettl3ΔIEC mice and genetic deletion of IRF7 restored the resistant phenotype of Mettl3ΔIEC mice to RV infection.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the genetic rescue experiments.

claim: Genetic deletion of IRF7 restored the resistant phenotype of Mettl3ΔIEC mice to RV infection.
source: Therefore, IRF7 is an important mediator of the increased IFNs and ISGs expression in Mettl3ΔIEC mice and genetic deletion of IRF7 restored the resistant phenotype of Mettl3ΔIEC mice to RV infection.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the genetic rescue experiments.

claim: The protein levels of the methyltransferases METTL3 and METTL14 and demethylase FTO were not affected by RV infection in ileum tissue.
source: The protein levels of the methyltransferases METTL3 and METTL14 and demethylase FTO were not affected by RV infection in ileum tissue (Figure 4a and b).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4a and b.

claim: The protein level of demethylase ALKBH5 was significantly down-regulated by RV infection in the ileum.
source: In contrast, the protein level of demethylase ALKBH5 was significantly down-regulated by RV infection in the ileum (Figure 4a and b).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4a and b.

claim: The depletion of ALKBH5 in IECs did not affect the anti-RV immune response.
source: The depletion of ALKBH5 in IECs did not affected the anti-RV immune response (Figure 4c), the viral shedding in the feces (Figure 4d), or the viral protein expression in the ileum (Figure 4e), likely due to the suppressed ALKBH5 expression in ileum tissue of WT mice infected by RV.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data from Alkbh5ΔIEC mice shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The depletion of ALKBH5 in IECs did not affect the viral shedding in the feces.
source: The depletion of ALKBH5 in IECs did not affected the anti-RV immune response (Figure 4c), the viral shedding in the feces (Figure 4d), or the viral protein expression in the ileum (Figure 4e), likely due to the suppressed ALKBH5 expression in ileum tissue of WT mice infected by RV.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data from Alkbh5ΔIEC mice shown in Figure 4d.

claim: The depletion of ALKBH5 in IECs did not affect the viral protein expression in the ileum.
source: The depletion of ALKBH5 in IECs did not affected the anti-RV immune response (Figure 4c), the viral shedding in the feces (Figure 4d), or the viral protein expression in the ileum (Figure 4e), likely due to the suppressed ALKBH5 expression in ileum tissue of WT mice infected by RV.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data from Alkbh5ΔIEC mice shown in Figure 4e.

claim: The lack of phenotype in Alkbh5ΔIEC mice is likely due to the suppressed ALKBH5 expression in ileum tissue of WT mice infected by RV.
source: The depletion of ALKBH5 in IECs did not affected the anti-RV immune response (Figure 4c), the viral shedding in the feces (Figure 4d), or the viral protein expression in the ileum (Figure 4e), likely due to the suppressed ALKBH5 expression in ileum tissue of WT mice infected by RV.
evidence: This is an inference to explain the lack of phenotype in Alkbh5ΔIEC mice.

claim: The Alkbh5 expression is much higher than Fto in intestine.
source: We found the Alkbh5/ALKBH5 expression is much higher than Fto/FTO in intestine (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq and qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a.

claim: ALKBH5 but not FTO is the dominant m6A eraser in IECs.
source: Through dot blot assay, we found ALKBH5 but not FTO is the dominant m6A eraser in IECs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by dot blot data from knockdown experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Overexpressing of recombinant ALKBH5 increased the IFN/ISGs response and inhibit RRV infection in mouse IEC MODE-K cells.
source: Furthermore, overexpressing of recombinant ALKBH5 increased the IFN/ISGs response and inhibit RRV infection in mouse IEC MODE-K cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), suggesting re-expression of ALKBH5 might overcome the immune evasion of RV.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data from overexpression experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Re-expression of ALKBH5 might overcome the immune evasion of RV.
source: Furthermore, overexpressing of recombinant ALKBH5 increased the IFN/ISGs response and inhibit RRV infection in mouse IEC MODE-K cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), suggesting re-expression of ALKBH5 might overcome the immune evasion of RV.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the overexpression experiment results.

claim: Non-structural protein 1 (NSP1) is a well-established RV-encoded innate immune antagonist that are showed to degrade IRF3 and β-Trcp.
source: Non-structural protein 1 (NSP1) is a well-established RV-encoded innate immune antagonist that are showed to degrade IRF3 and β-Trcp (Barro and Patton, 2005; Ding et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Only WT RV reduced ALKBH5 protein levels, not NSP1-null RV.
source: We infected HEK293 cells with WT and NSP1-null RVs, only WT RV reduced ALKBH5 protein levels (Figure 4f), suggesting that the down-regulation of ALKBH5 expression by RV is NSP1-dependent.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data comparing WT and NSP1-null RV shown in Figure 4f.

claim: The down-regulation of ALKBH5 expression by RV is NSP1-dependent.
source: We infected HEK293 cells with WT and NSP1-null RVs, only WT RV reduced ALKBH5 protein levels (Figure 4f), suggesting that the down-regulation of ALKBH5 expression by RV is NSP1-dependent.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of WT and NSP1-null RV effects.

claim: RV might evade the antiviral immune response via downregulation of ALKBH5 expression by NSP1.
source: These results suggest that RV might evades the antiviral immune response via downregulation of ALKBH5 expression by NSP1.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the NSP1-dependent ALKBH5 downregulation.

claim: Previous studies reported that m6A modifications on mRNA in mice embryonic fibroblasts or normal human dermal fibroblasts negatively regulate the IFN response by accelerating the mRNA degradation of type I IFNs.
source: Previous studies reported that m6A modifications on mRNA in mice embryonic fibroblasts or normal human dermal fibroblasts negatively regulate the IFN response by accelerating the mRNA degradation of type I IFNs (Rubio et al., 2018; Winkler et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Type I and type III IFNs play a critical role in the antiviral immune response in the GI tract.
source: Since type I and type III IFNs play a critical role in the antiviral immune response in the GI tract (Pott et al., 2011), we used an RV infection model, in which IECs are specifically infected, as well as conditional knockout mice with IECs-specific depletion of m6A writer METTL3 or m6A eraser ALKBH5, to study the role of m6A modification in regulating IFN response towards rotavirus in IECs.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: m6A modification is known to affect viral gene expression, replication, and generation of progeny virions.
source: In addition to directly regulating target genes that involved in innate immune pathways, m6A modification is also known to affect viral gene expression, replication, and generation of progeny virions (Roundtree et al., 2017; Brocard et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Some viral RNA genomes are modified by m6A, such as simian virus 40, influenza A virus, adenovirus, avian sarcoma virus, Rous Sarcoma virus, hepatitis C virus and Zika virus.
source: Some viral RNA genomes are modified by m6A, such as simian virus 40 (Tsai et al., 2018; Lavi and Shatkin, 1975), influenza A virus (Krug et al., 1976), adenovirus (Sommer et al., 1976), avian sarcoma virus (Dimock and Stoltzfus, 1977), Rous Sarcoma virus (Kane and Beemon, 1985), hepatitis C virus (Gokhale et al., 2016) and Zika virus (Lichinchi et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Rotavirus RNA has m6A modification.
source: Through our m6A-RIP-qPCR, Rotavirus RNA was also found to have m6A modification (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by m6A-RIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Genetic deletion of METTL3 in monkey kidney MA104 cell line led to reduced RV replication.
source: Of note, genetic deletion of METTL3 in monkey kidney MA104 cell line, which has limited IFN responses (Sánchez-Tacuba et al., 2020), also led to reduced RV replication (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data from MA104 cells shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: MA104 cell line has limited IFN responses.
source: Of note, genetic deletion of METTL3 in monkey kidney MA104 cell line, which has limited IFN responses (Sánchez-Tacuba et al., 2020), also led to reduced RV replication (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: IRF7 deficiency didn't fully restore the suppressed rotaviral infection in Mettl3ΔIEC mice.
source: Further, IRF7 deficiency didn't fully restore the suppressed rotaviral infection in Mettl3ΔIEC mice (Figure 3e).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: m6A modifications were shown to maintain the genomic stability of mice embryonic stem cells by promoting the degradation of endogenous retrovirus (ERV) mRNA, or by regulating ERV heterochromatin and inhibiting its transcription.
source: Intriguingly, m6A modifications were shown to maintain the genomic stability of mice embryonic stem cells by promoting the degradation of endogenous retrovirus (ERV) mRNA, or by regulating ERV heterochromatin and inhibiting its transcription (Xu et al., 2021; Chelmicki et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The absence of m6A results in the formation of abnormal endogenous dsRNA, which causes an aberrant immune response and necrosis in the hematopoietic system.
source: The absence of m6A results in the formation of abnormal endogenous dsRNA, which causes an aberrant immune response and necrosis in the hematopoietic system (Gao et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: There is an increase of dsRNA levels in IECs of Mettl3ΔIEC mice compared to the littermate WT mice.
source: In the intestine, through immunostaining with J2 antibody, we detected the increase of dsRNA levels in IECs of Mettl3ΔIEC mice compare to the littermate WT mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: In the absence of METTL3, the increase of dsRNA will induce the IFN responses, and the increased stability of Irf7 mRNA will amplify this process.
source: Our data suggest a dual activation model in steady state that in the absence of METTL3, the increase of dsRNA will induce the IFN responses, and the increased stability of Irf7 mRNA, which serves as a key transcription factor of IFN and ISG expression, will amplify this process.
evidence: This is a mechanistic model proposed based on the experimental data.

claim: m6A modification of viral RNA genomes affect the activation of innate sensor-mediated signaling.
source: Furthermore, m6A modification of viral RNA genomes affect the activation of innate sensor-mediated signaling (Chen et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Decreased m6A modification on RV genomes may activate innate sensors directly and induce higher IFN response, which will also be amplified by increase of Irf7 mRNA stability.
source: Decreased m6A modification on RV genomes may activate innate sensors directly and induce higher IFN response, which will also be amplified by increase of Irf7 mRNA stability.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic explanation for the observed phenotypes.

claim: RV infection down-regulates the level of m6A eraser ALKBH5 to induce m6A modifications, in an NSP1 dependent manner.
source: Here, we found RV infection down-regulates the level of m6A eraser ALKBH5 to induce m6A modifications, in an NSP1 dependent manner.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental data presented.

claim: ALKBH5 deficiency in IECs results in normal susceptibility to RV infection.
source: As a result, ALKBH5 deficiency in IECs results in normal susceptibility to RV infection.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental data from Alkbh5ΔIEC mice.

claim: The dual regulation of m6A levels during RV infection and development provide new insights into the choice of either RV or the host on regulation of m6A modification to achieve either immune evasion or immune surveillance, respectively.
source: The dual regulation of m6A levels during RV infection and development provide new insights into the choice of either RV or the host on regulation of m6A modification to achieve either immune evasion or immune surveillance, respectively.
evidence: This is an interpretive statement about the broader implications of the findings.
